q: What are the three steps of a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: Divide into subproblems, conquer them recursively, combine the results
explain: Merge sort divides the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and combines them with merge.

q: What is merge sort's running time on an array of n elements?
options: Θ(n log n) in the best, average and worst case
explain: The split is always into halves, whatever the data, so the recursion has log n levels with Θ(n) merge work on each.
There are two half-size subproblems plus a linear merge. T(n − 1) + n is selection sort or worst-case quicksort, and T(n/2) + 1 is binary search.

q: Two sorted lists with m and n elements are merged. What is the maximum number of comparisons?
explain: Each comparison outputs one element. The last element is always output without a comparison, once one list is empty.

q: Using the master theorem, solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n.
explain: Here n^(log₂ 4) = n², and f(n) = n is polynomially smaller, so case 1 applies: Θ(n²).

q: Using the master theorem, solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n².
explain: Here n^(log₂ 2) = n, and f(n) = n² is polynomially larger (with the regularity condition holding), so case 3 applies: Θ(n²).

q: Standard merge sort on an array is an in-place sorting algorithm.
explain: False. The merge step needs Θ(n) extra space for the output. Heapsort and quicksort are (nearly) in-place.

q: Why does merge take from the left list when left[i] == right[j]?
options: It keeps equal keys in their original order, which makes the sort stable
explain: Stability matters when sorting records by one field after another. Taking the right element first on ties would still sort correctly, but stability would be lost.

q: How many inversions does the array [2, 4, 1, 3, 5] have?
explain: The inversions are the pairs (2, 1), (4, 1) and (4, 3). Merge sort counts them during merging: when a right element is taken, it forms an inversion with every remaining left element.

q: Why does the master theorem not apply to T(n) = T(n − 1) + n?
options: The subproblem is n − 1, not n/b for a constant b > 1
Because f(n) = n is too large
It does apply, giving Θ(n log n)
explain: The master theorem needs subproblems that shrink by a constant factor. Unrolling gives n + (n − 1) + … + 1 = Θ(n²).
